section_summary.evidence_source: 1. Introduction Historically, body image research has focused on negative body image. Although important for understanding the pervasiveness of body concerns and potentially associated eating problems,this narrow focus failed to address the complexity of thoughts and feelings people may have about their bodies, including positive perceptions. Recent research has indicated that positive body image is in fact a separate construct from negative body image, with its own unique dimensions and correlates (Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). Tylka and Wood-Barcalow (2015a) define positive body image as body appreciation, loving and feeling comfort with one's body, having broad ideas of attractiveness, adaptive self-care for appearance, manifesting positive feelings through the body, and filtering information about the body in protective ways. Psychometrically sound measures have been developed to capture these constructs including body appreciation, the most widely studied aspect of positive body image (Avalos, Tylka, & Wood-Barcalow, 2005; Tylka & Wood-Barcalow, 2015a). The current study focused on associations between body appreciation and putative correlates that relate to the desire to enhance or to express one's appearance.
